method: Mostly I slowed down. Instead of skimming, I read each source critically and wrote questions in the margins, asking what it assumes and who it leaves out. Then I used the idea cards to force new angles on my project, gathered images into a moodboard, and in code rebuilt a simple multi-page site and added my first JavaScript.
related_work: I read the week's material through a critical lens, treating every source as an argument to question rather than information to absorb. On sustainability, EşiDİR et al. show Apple's carbon-neutral Watch claims lean on carbon credits and sit uneasily next to ongoing litigation. Fakhredin and Campean's repairer study, the UK Parliament's e-waste report and iFixit's teardown all point to the same physical reality: glued, fused designs that resist repair. Crawford's Atlas of AI and the news reports on student labour and supplier automation connect the watch's 'smart' surface to the mines and factories behind it, while Mintel adds the demand side. Together these gave my project its critical backbone.

conclusion_future_work: My takeaway is that reading critically and designing are the same habit: don't accept the first version, ask what it assumes and what it hides. That is exactly the question my Digital Archaeology project now sits on. Next week I want to push the project further and keep the same critical eye on my own work.
results_discussion: The critical reading did the heavy lifting. Reading Apple's carbon-neutral claims against a repairer's teardown and a government e-waste report showed me that a product's marketing and its material reality can say completely different things, and that became the spine of my project. I built a moodboard as an evidence wall for Digital Archaeology, a site about a discarded smartwatch and the hidden costs inside it: the lithium, the data centre, the factory. The idea cards pushed me past my first idea into that deeper question about what is left behind after convenience is used up. On the coding side I had done some C# before, but this week the underlying logic finally clicked: HTML gives structure, CSS gives style, JavaScript gives behaviour. What is still unresolved is making the writing and the making feed each other, so the moodboard is not just decoration but actually drives the page.
title: Critical reading, idea cards, and a moodboard
introduction: This week Creative Tech 1 moved from setting up to actually thinking and designing. We learned how to read literature critically instead of just skimming it, and we used idea cards to push our project thinking further. I also built a moodboard for my project, while the coding side got into the basics of making a webpage with HTML, CSS and a first bit of JavaScript.
